author: Monthly Review Press
title: New! “Grand Theft Capital”, by Fred Magdoff and John Bellamy Foster
content:
A 

New York Times

 headline in early 2026 announced what many workers have known for years: “For Many Cash-Strapped Americans, ‘Basic Living has become a Burden.’” Living paycheck-to-paycheck, with little or no savings for emergencies, workers are struggling to make ends meet. It should come as no surprise that, without a clear sense of the problem’s source, workers are left blaming easy targets: immigrants, people of color, religious minorities, or damaging decisions by a few, corporate bad apples.




But as 

Grand Theft Capital 

demonstrates, workers’ current conditions are the result of a deliberate, long-term effort by the corporate rich to increase their own wealth largely by extracting it from workers’ pockets. The evidence shows that workers’ wages have not kept pace with rising costs and that they’re feeling unhappy and stressed on the job. This partly reflects the weakening of worker power as union membership has declined over the past sixty years—reaching levels last seen before the major unionization wave of the 1930s. Regardless of what mainstream economists and the Consumer Price Index suggest, successive generations of young workers have been confronting difficult and precarious employment conditions. On top of it all, workers of all generations are alarmed at the possibility of job obsolescence given the looming threat of AI and automation.

title: New: “‘Black Marxism’: A Marxist Critique”, by August Nimtz
content:
Over the last decade, Cedric Robinson’s 

Black Marxism: The Making of the Black Radical Tradition

 has deeply shaped debates on the place of race within capitalist societies. Perhaps these questions are now settled, but at one time they were far too controversial: 




  Is race subsumed by class, with the latter the sine qua non of capitalism?   




Do race and class act independently within modern societies?   




Or does capitalism inevitably express a deeper racial impetus in the West?




August Nimtz defends Marxism from Robinson’s accusations of myopia on matters of race, suggesting that, in charging Marx and Engels with Eurocentrism, he either failed to understand, or misrepresented, their work—and that, in effect, many thinkers inspired by 

Black Marxism

 blatantly misrepresented Marxist texts…

title: New: “Requiem for French Theory” by Aymeric Monville, Jennifer Ponce de León and Gabriel Rockhill
content:
In the public eye: “Requiem for French Theory”




Coming from Left Field

 (Episode 152)




In this episode of Coming From Left Field, philosopher and cultural critic Gabriel Rockhill joins 

Greg Godels & Pat Cummings

 to explore the Ford Foundation, the 1966 Johns Hopkins conference often cited as a launching point for French Theory in the United States, Cold War cultural politics, and the wider political economy of academic knowledge production. Rockhill argues for rebuilding a class-centered, internationalist Marxism and joins a thoughtful exchange on China, Vietnam, socialism, imperialism, inequality, and the challenges of assessing existing socialist projects without demonization or uncritical celebration….

author: Monthly Review Press
title: Recently reissued: The Rainbow Challenge (Excerpt)
content:
From the Preface to the new edition of 

The Rainbow Challenge

:




“Jesse Jackson’s first presidential primary race in 1984 should have been a wakeup call for the Democratic Party. Without a large campaign chest, money for advertising, or seasoned political consultants he amassed 3.5 million votes (winning nearly the entire popular vote in the Deep South states of Mississippi and South Carolina, registering 2 million new voters, and winning 21 percent of the total votes cast). The press, the pundits, the pollsters, and the Democratic Party elites could not believe that the American people would vote for a Black man, let alone a man with such a progressive message, so they characterized him at first as a charlatan, then as a spoiler, and finally as a candidate who spoke only for African Americans. They had accepted the idea that Ronald Reagan’s election in 1980 meant that the New Deal reforms were over, that the growing polarization of the electorate could not be overcome, and that the Great Society had been defeated. Their marginalization of Jackson’s message of economic and social justice and international peace through cooperation, and their failure to imagine that anything else could be different, ceded the playing field to the Republican right. Walter Mondale’s tepid, neoliberal message could not compete with Reagan’s sunny, simplistic optimism; Reagan won by a landslide

author: Monthly Review Press
title: In the Public Eye: “Albert Einstein’s ‘Why Socialism?'”
content:
London Review of Books

: Letters section features a quote from  John Bellamy Foster’s introduction to the book:




“…Einstein’s essay ‘Why Socialism?’, published in 1949 in the first issue of 

Monthly Review

, remains one of the most succinct and powerful arguments for socialism ever written. ‘The crippling of the social consciousness,’ Einstein wrote, is ‘the worst evil of capitalism’. ‘I am convinced’, he concluded, ‘there is only one way to eliminate these grave evils, namely through the establishment of a socialist economy.’




‘Why Socialism?’ was regarded by the FBI as direct confirmation of what they referred to as Einstein’s strong ‘communist sympathies’. The Bureau had opened a file on him in late 1932, when he was in the US on a visitor’s visa to teach at Caltech, with a long report by the Woman Patriot Corporation arguing that he should not be admitted to the country. ‘Not even Stalin himself,’ the WPC charged, ‘is affiliated with so many anarcho-communist international groups to promote … world revolution and ultimate anarchy, as ALBERT EINSTEIN.’ The FBI continued to collect everything it could on Einstein’s socialist connections for the remainder of his life.”

title: New! Chris dePloeg’s “The Exterminating Empire”
content:
REVIEWS:




Counterpunch

, “

Capitalism is Waging War on Palestine While Creating a Burning Planet

” by Daniel Falcone:




Daniel Falcone: 

What is the central argument of 

The Exterminating Empire

 and how is the book structured? It looks as though the book serves as an intervention as well as an addition to current scholarship.  




Chris Kaspar de Ploeg:

 I open the book with some jarring facts that seem paradoxical at first sight. We need about 30 percent of our productive capacity to 

give everyone on the planet a good life

. Not just the basics like housing, clothing and healthcare, but also modern appliances like refrigerators, laptops, access to the internet and more. At the same time, that standard of living is denied to about 

80 percent of the world population

. Green energy has been cheaper than fossil fuels for years, yet climate breakdown is only accelerating. We could 

solve world hunger

 with about 0.03 percent of global GDP, but hunger is only increasing.




That looks like an extraordinarily wasteful system, and it is. The point, however, is that under capitalism, these are not paradoxes at all. In fact, they are signs of capital’s success. Under our current economic system, the primary goal, ruthlessly pursued, is
